analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal labor law to weaken unions and make it easier to treat workers as contractors.
analysis.headline: The Employee Rights Act, introduced with 14 House Republican sponsors in June 2025, has sat in two House committees with no hearing, no vote, and no movement since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act and related labor laws. It would require NLRB-run secret-ballot elections before workers get a union, bar workers without lawful immigration status from voting in union elections, and require unions to get written, annually renewed permission before spending dues on anything beyond bargaining and contract administration. It would also lock in a loose test for who counts as an independent contractor, sharply narrow when two companies count as a single "joint employer" — including a carve-out protecting franchisors like fast-food headquarters — and let workers in right-to-work states opt out of union bargaining and negotiate individually. It has been referred to two House committees and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, most of all. Franchise chains gain insulation from liability for franchisee workplaces. Gig platforms and businesses that rely on contractors gain a codified, looser test that keeps workers out of employee status (minimum wage, overtime, and union rights). Employers fighting union drives gain elections, voter-list limits, and opt-in dues rules that make organizing and sustaining unions harder. A narrower group also benefits: individual workers in right-to-work states who would rather negotiate on their own than be covered by a union contract.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Franchise chains, gig platforms, and anti-union employers

how_it_helps.text: Codifies a two-part independent-contractor test and bars regulators from counting supervision, safety rules, insurance requirements, or deadlines as evidence of employment, keeping many workers out of minimum-wage, overtime, and union protections [S2].

Narrows joint-employer status to companies that directly, actually, and immediately control essential terms of employment, and flatly provides that handing franchisees a handbook or harassment policy cannot make a franchisor an employer [S2].
Requires that union representation be chosen in a secret-ballot election run by the NLRB, foreclosing card-check recognition agreements [S2].

Requires written, annually renewed employee authorization before any dues can be spent on non-bargaining activities, and makes union misuse of workers' personal contact information an unfair labor practice [S2].
Lets workers in right-to-work ('covered') states leave the bargaining unit and negotiate individually, and bars collective bargaining agreements from including DEI provisions [S2].
Exempts tribes and tribally owned businesses on tribal land from the National Labor Relations Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, the cost falls on workers who rely on collective bargaining: unions lose dues revenue and bargaining leverage, union contracts shrink to the members who stay, and workers reclassified as independent contractors lose minimum wage, overtime, and the right to organize. Workers in industries like agriculture and construction who lack lawful status would lose any vote on their representation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unionized workers and workers seeking employee status

drawbacks.text: Loosening the contractor test and narrowing joint-employer status shifts workers off the books that carry minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance, and bargaining rights — misclassification disputes have historically been a major source of wage theft claims [S2].

Letting employees opt out of bargaining units in right-to-work states ('independent negotiating') would fragment contracts and could pull wages and benefits toward whatever an individual worker can extract alone [S2].

The opt-in rule for non-bargaining dues, with annual expiration, would cut the funding unions use for political and public advocacy — a real cost to unions, though framed as protecting members' money [S2].

Rewriting the federal extortion statute with a carve-out for 'minor' injury or damage during peaceful picketing, prosecutable only by states, narrows federal tools against violence in labor disputes [S2].

Supporters' strongest counterargument: secret-ballot elections, private ballots on dues, and the right to negotiate individually are genuine employee freedoms, and the franchisor provisions protect small franchise owners from being held liable for rules headquarters imposes on them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers some real protections — privacy limits on organizers' contact lists and a worker-chosen form of contact information — and individual choice is a fair value. But the provisions with the largest reach all move power one direction: toward employers. A looser contractor test and a narrower joint-employer standard determine whether millions of workers get basic wage-and-hour protections at all, and the individual-negotiating and dues provisions shrink unions' ability to bargain. Weighed honestly, the gains to individual choice are small next to the loss of bargaining power and workplace protections for the broader workforce.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in June 2025, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen introduced the Employee Rights Act in the House on June 26, 2025 [S1].
Thirteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Judiciary Committee, where provisions fall by jurisdiction [S4].
Since the referral, the action history shows no hearings, no committee votes, and no floor action [S4].
Congress remains in session through January 2027, so the bill is still technically alive [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained, because nothing has passed. If the bill stays stalled, the biggest winners are unionized workers and workers seeking employee status, whose current protections remain intact; employers who would benefit from the bill are the ones kept waiting.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Republican — 14 of 223 — and no Democrat has signed on; the bill has not advanced in the Republican-run committees either.

industries.note: The bill writes a narrow joint-employer standard into law and provides that giving franchisees handbooks or harassment policies can never make the franchisor an employer. That shields corporate headquarters from liability when franchisee workers are underpaid or mistreated, and leaves those workers with no one above the franchisee to bargain with.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and businesses built on contractors (rideshare, delivery, cleaning)
industries.note: The bill codifies a looser independent-contractor test and forbids counting supervision, deadlines, insurance, or safety rules as evidence of employment. Workers classified out of employee status lose minimum wage, overtime, and the right to unionize, which lowers these companies' labor costs.

Secret-ballot election requirements, restricted voter lists, opt-in dues with annual re-authorization, individual negotiating in right-to-work states, and a ban on DEI contract provisions would all shrink union membership, finances, and bargaining power. Unions' interest here runs alongside the workers they represent, since weaker unions mean weaker contracts.

The narrow joint-employer test means a client company that supervises temp workers day-to-day but formally employs them through an agency is likely not a joint employer, cutting the agencies' and clients' exposure to labor-law liability that workers would otherwise claim against both.

industries.industry: Tribal enterprises (casinos and tribally owned businesses)
industries.note: The bill exempts tribes and tribally owned businesses on tribal land from the National Labor Relations Act. Presented as tribal sovereignty, it also means tribal employees would have no federal right to organize or bargain.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has 14 Republican sponsors in a 223-member Republican House conference, and neither committee has taken it up after six months. Prior Congresses' versions of the Employee Rights Act have never reached a floor vote. With no hearing scheduled and competing priorities on the majority's calendar, the most likely path is that it stays in committee and dies when this Congress ends in January 2027.
